name: Carnosine
lead: Carnosine (beta-alanyl-L-histidine) is a dipeptide of beta-alanine and histidine found at high concentrations in skeletal muscle and brain, and in meat; it is not found in plant foods [1][2][3]. It is sold as an oral supplement and added to some skincare products, where it is positioned for antioxidant and anti-glycation effects, meaning protection against the sugar-driven cross-linking of proteins such as collagen [1][4].

Laboratory work has shown that carnosine scavenges reactive oxygen species, chelates metal ions, buffers pH and reduces formation of advanced glycation end-products [3][5]. Evidence for visible skin improvement in people is limited, and the best human evidence for the carnosine pathway concerns beta-alanine supplementation, which raises muscle carnosine and has been studied for exercise performance [6][7][8].
infobox: Meat and fish; made in the body from beta-alanine and histidine [1][2]

paras: Wikipedia notes that carnosine-containing products are used in topical preparations aimed at wrinkles, and describes carnosine as a proposed geroprotector on the basis of its anti-glycation activity and cell-culture findings of an extended fibroblast lifespan and slower telomere shortening; the same article observes that telomere preservation could in theory favour certain cancers [1]. A 2025 cosmetic-chemistry paper on a newly synthesised antioxidant with anti-glycation activity is among the skin-focused work in this area [9].

Beta-alanine is the limiting precursor, so supplementing it raises muscle carnosine concentration; the International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand reports that several weeks of supplementation raise muscle carnosine and improve performance in efforts lasting about one to four minutes [1][6][10]. Carnosine itself has been tested in small trials for conditions including Gulf War illness, cognitive function and several metabolic and vascular conditions [11][12][13].
No randomised trial of topical or oral carnosine for visible skin ageing or wrinkles was identified in the available literature; skin-related evidence is largely laboratory-based [9][3].

Human trials of the related precursor are more extensive. A 2017 meta-analysis of 40 studies (1,461 participants) assessed beta-alanine supplementation and exercise performance, and a 2024 meta-analysis in trained young men reported an overall effect size of 0.39 in favour of beta-alanine for maximal-intensity exercise [7][8]. A 2024 trial examined beta-alanine in high-intensity functional training [14].

Carnosine itself has been studied in small randomised trials in other settings, such as Gulf War illness and cognitive function in older adults, and ClinicalTrials.gov lists registered trials in peripheral arterial disease, diabetic neuropathy, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and type 2 diabetes [11][12][15][16][17][18][19][20]. A 2023 narrative review assessed carnosine and beta-alanine supplementation across human medicine [21].

Carnosine is made by carnosine synthase from beta-alanine and histidine, with beta-alanine the rate-limiting component [1][2]. A comprehensive 2013 review describes its pH-buffering, metal-chelating, antioxidant and anti-glycation properties and the role of the carnosine-degrading enzyme serum carnosinase [3]. Peroxyl-radical trapping by carnosine was characterised in a 1988 paper [22]. Oral carnosine is broken down by carnosinases, which is why beta-alanine is the form used to raise muscle levels [1][23].

The sports nutrition position stand describes beta-alanine as safe in healthy people at recommended intakes, with paraesthesia (tingling) the only reported side effect, reduced by divided doses or sustained-release forms [6]. Long-term safety data for topical carnosine in cosmetics were not identified.

Carnosine was isolated in 1900 by Vladimir Gulevich from meat extract and named for its presence in flesh [1][2]. Synthesis from beta-alanine and histidine was characterised in the mid-20th century and its buffering role in muscle was studied in later decades [2].

On bodybuilding forums such as T Nation, carnosine and beta-alanine have been discussed since the early 2000s, typically in the context of multivitamin and recovery stacks and, in some posts, for anti-glycation or anti-ageing purposes [24][25][26][27][28].

timeline.event: Carnosine is discovered in meat extract by Vladimir Gulevich [1][2].
Antioxidant activity of carnosine and related dipeptides is reported in PNAS [22].
A major review of carnosine physiology and pathophysiology is published [3].
The International Society of Sports Nutrition issues a beta-alanine position stand [6].

lore.intro: Carnosine comes up on T Nation threads as a supplement within multi-ingredient stacks, as an anti-glycation compound, and in one quoted coaching remark about injectable use [24][25][26][27].

claims.claim: Carnosine fights glycation and is useful for anti-ageing
claims.believers: Posters on T Nation threads about glucose and anti-ageing supplements recommend carnosine, or beta-alanine to raise it, because of its reported anti-glycating effects [26][28].
claims.experts: Laboratory studies and reviews report that carnosine reduces advanced glycation end-product formation, but evidence that supplementation visibly slows human ageing is preliminary [3][1].

claims.claim: Beta-alanine raises muscle carnosine and improves high-intensity performance
claims.believers: A T Nation post summarises that beta-alanine raises muscle carnosine by up to 58 percent in four weeks, and users report using it before workouts [29].
claims.experts: Meta-analyses of placebo-controlled trials report small to moderate performance benefits, particularly in efforts of one to four minutes, and a position stand describes tingling as the main side effect [6][7][8].

claims.believers: A forum post quotes a strength coach saying that injectable L-carnosine and intravenous vitamin C were among key recovery methods in use at his facility [27].
claims.experts: No controlled trial of injected carnosine for athletic recovery was identified in the available literature.

claims.claim: Oral carnosine acts as a general antioxidant supplement in a stack
claims.believers: Several users list carnosine among supplements taken daily, and one reports it worked well alongside a pre-workout product [24][25][30].
claims.experts: Carnosine shows antioxidant activity in laboratory assays, while trials of oral carnosine in people are small and condition-specific [22][11][12].
